397.content: The price lookup over `table`. Keys match regardless of case.

398.content:
Table keys name one model each. A key prices a model whose id is the key, the key followed by a date (`-20250929`,
`-2025-08-07` or `@20250929`), or either after one `<provider>/` prefix: `claude-sonnet-4-5` prices
`claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`, `claude-sonnet-4-5@20250929` and `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5`. Any other ending
names another model, so `gpt-5` prices none of `gpt-5.7`, `gpt-5-codex` or `gpt-5-mini`, and `o1` does not price
`o1-mini`. Among the keys an id matches, the id itself wins, then the id without its date, then both without
the prefix.

399.content:
`fallback` keys are family aliases, used only when no table key matches: a model takes the longest fallback key its
id contains, the first given among equally long keys, so `opus` prices `claude-opus-4-9` and `gpt-5` prices
`gpt-5.7`.

400.content:
`overrides` are the caller's own rules and, unlike table keys, match by substring: a model takes the longest
override key its id contains, the first given among equally long keys, and that override wins over the table and
the fallback, so `{ opus: … }` reprices both `claude-opus-4-8` and `claude-3-opus`. A partial override takes the
prices it lacks from the price the id has without overrides: over a table with `gpt-4o` and `gpt-4o-2024-05-13`,
`{ "gpt-4o": { input: 1 } }` keeps the dated model's own output price. A partial override of an id without a price
of its own gives no price. An override entry that says nothing about `longContext` keeps the model's own tier, and
one with a `longContext` replaces it. A model that nothing prices has no price. Lookups are cached by model id.

404.content:
The record by model, priced: one part per model of its split, or the whole record as one part. `summarize` and
`costOf` charge records through it. A part's cost follows three rules in order: (1) an amount the part carries
(`costUsd`), such as one the agent logged, wins; (2) otherwise each token count is charged at the model's price;
(3) that amount is multiplied by the record's `pricingMultiplier`. An agent's own amount is what it billed, so the
multiplier does not apply to it. A count the part lacks costs nothing; a part without a model, or with a model that
the pricing does not know, has no cost: absent, never 0.

405.content:
A split replaces the aggregate, never adds to it, and wins over it: when the agent logged an amount for the record
and for every model, the models' amounts are used. The record stays whole only when the agent logged an amount for
it that the split does not divide among every model, because charging the other models at table prices would
replace the agent's amount. An amount from a price table on a split record, as `{ ...record, ...costOf(record,
pricing) }` leaves it, does not keep the record whole: its models are charged again. A part of a split counts the
model calls its share records, not a portion of the record's.

406.content:
The long-context tier prices one request. A `request` record is one; a `turn` or `session` record, and each part
of one, is an aggregate of several calls, whose totals cannot tell how large any single request's context was,
so it bills at the base rates and never at an average — the same limit ccusage's aggregation states for its
summed totals. An aggregate counts as one request only when its own, or a part's, `modelCalls` is 1.

410.content:
Totals of `records` in the window, as presence summarizes its sources: tokens, how many records contributed, and
the sum of the costs that `priceRecord` gives their parts, per group. A group's cost is absent when none of its
parts had a cost; parts without one add their tokens but no dollars. The total adds up the groups, as presence adds
up its sources, and counts each record once. A record split by model (`usageByModel`) adds its split, model by
model, and not its aggregate as well, so a turn of several models counts its tokens once and each model's tokens
land in that model's group.

415.content:

priced record; `priceRecord` gives a record split by model one per model.

416.content: One model's share of a record split by model, or the whole record, with its cost when something prices it.

880.content:
Applies a plan from `planInstall` once. Under the scope's LedgerLock it probes what an earlier holder left pending,
refuses the plan when the ledger moved on since it was built or when any target no longer holds what the plan saw
(nothing is written then), and otherwise runs the steps with the guarantees of `applyLocked`. The lock is released
only after the step in flight finished and its outcome was recorded.

881.content:
Writes into files that agents and other tools share are not compare-and-swap: a writer that does not take the
LedgerLock can still change a file between the re-check and the write, and that change is lost without a trace.

885.content: Drops a plan without applying it; applying it afterwards fails with `PlanStale`.

888.content:
Reports, without changing anything an agent reads: whether the ledger is readable and has unfinished operations,
whether the LedgerLock is free (and what its holder recorded), owned Artifacts that drifted from the ledger or are
broken symlinks, and the command hooks each agent loads (its settings files and every plugin's or extension's hooks
file, plus the other agents' files it runs) that never run (unknown events), use the wrong timeout unit, point at a
missing program whose first word `shell-quote` reads as a certain absolute path, or fire twice for one event: the
same command twice, or, given `markers`, two hooks of one application, such as an old hook in a settings file next
to the plugin that replaced it. Taking the lock to test it creates the lock files in the harness state directory
and nothing else.

891.content: What the scope's ledger records, read without the lock; it may change right after.

896.content:
Plans the installation of a bundle into agents, without writing: renders the bundle with each agent's preferred
strategy (hooks placed so that no event fires twice in an agent that runs another agent's hooks), reads what is on
disk and in the ledger, and checks the plan invariants. A plan with a conflict and no explicit choice fails with
`PlanConflict`, listing the choices that would resolve each. When an earlier change left operations pending, it
takes the LedgerLock long enough to probe and settle them first.

900.content:
Removes what the ledger records for an owner, under one holding of the LedgerLock: plans the removal (an install
plan in which the owner wants nothing) against the ledger read under the lock and applies it at once. Only the
owner's entries go: a file harness created is deleted, a pre-image restored, an entry other owners or agents still
use released, and an Artifact the user changed since is kept and reported. Empty shared configuration files are
deleted only with recorded file-creation provenance; pre-existing files and implicit parent directories stay.
With `legacyMarkers`, what older versions
of the owner left without a ledger is removed as well. Nothing is written at a path a dotfiles manager owns or
through a symlink; such steps are notes of the plan.

904.content:
Compares the owner's Artifacts on disk with the ledger and, given the bundle, with what it wants, the way chezmoi
does (see `verifyOwner`). Reading needs no lock; only when the ledger is behind the disk does verify take the
LedgerLock, compare again under it and record the disk's hash (`acknowledge`).

application reports it as `ObservedArtifact.symlinkTarget`, and a step that would write or delete through it is a

1178.content:
The fallback repository for platforms without SQLite: one JSON record per key, `<key>.lease.json`, replaced with

reports `busy` when the guard stays held longer than a second; `fence` holds `<key>.lease.fence`. Both are process
locks, so without SQLite they are lock files whose dead holders are reclaimed one reclaimer at a time, with the
gaps `acquireProcessLock` documents. A record with an unknown `schemaVersion` or shape is refused and never
overwritten.

1181.content:

1183.content:
The lease repository for one machine: one row per key in a SQLite database. `save` runs in a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`
transaction, which takes SQLite's write lock (an fcntl lock) before reading the revision, so processes sharing the
file compare and write atomically. The lock is released when its process exits, so neither a crashed writer nor a
reused pid can leave the repository stuck. Fails to build with `unavailable` when the platform has no SQLite, and
with `unsupported-schema` for a database written by a newer version.

1192.content: A lease duration is out of range, or the heartbeat does not fit twice into the TTL.

1193.content: A held lease. It belongs to the Scope `acquire` ran in: closing the Scope stops the heartbeat and releases it.

1194.content:
Fails with `LeaseLost` once the heartbeat finds the lease taken over, released or missing, or cannot confirm a
renewal within the TTL; it never succeeds. Race other work against it to stop that work on loss.

1195.content:
Runs `work` under the repository's per-key fence, after re-reading that this acquisition still holds the lease, and
passes it the fencing token for the writes it makes. Waiting for the fence stops when the lease is lost. When the
lease is lost while `work` runs, `work` is interrupted and the result fails with `LeaseLost`.

1196.content:
The fence is released when `work`'s fiber has ended, so a successor's fenced work starts only after that. An
interrupted fiber ends at once, though, while a Promise it started (`Effect.tryPromise`) keeps running: put a
write that cannot be cancelled in `Effect.uninterruptible`, which keeps the fence until the write settles, or pass
it the AbortSignal `tryPromise` provides and settle only after the write has stopped. A resource that can compare
atomically should also store the highest generation per token key and reject smaller generations in that write.

1290.content:
A single-instance lock on `path`, which must be in an existing local directory (not NFS). With `platform.sqlite`,
`path` is a SQLite database held with `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`: the kernel releases it when the process exits or
crashes, at once, and nothing is ever reclaimed. The holder's identity goes into `<path>.holder` for diagnostics
only, so a process that cannot read its own identity (`platform.process.self` throws: always on win32, which is not
supported, and on darwin in a sandbox that denies running `ps` or `sysctl`) still takes the lock: its `holder` is
`undefined`, and instead of writing `<path>.holder` it removes one that a dead holder left. Without SQLite, `path` is
a lock file that holds the identity itself; a lock file whose holder died is reclaimed on the next attempt, which
needs the holder on this host (see `tryFileLock` for the remaining gaps). The lock file cannot go without the
identity: the call rejects with the error reading it, and takes nothing.

1291.content:
Acquisitions of one lock in this process take turns in memory (see `takeTurn`): while one holds the lock or is
attempting it, the next waits for it to release the lock or give up, then makes its own attempt, so none of them
blocks the thread in a SQLite busy wait on a holder in this process. Without `wait`, a call that finds the turn taken
resolves to `ProcessLockHeld` at once, without attempting, with the holder read from the lock's record.

1301.content:
Whether another process, or an acquisition in this one, holds the process lock on `path`, checked without taking
it: the check writes nothing (no `<path>.holder`, and a missing lock file stays missing and reads as free). The
answer may be stale by the time it arrives, so it can choose between handing work to the holder and starting one,
but it does not replace acquiring. The check never waits, so `signal` is consulted once, before it starts: an
aborted signal rejects with `signal.reason` without touching the lock file.

1302.content:
With `platform.sqlite` it makes one attempt at a shared lock on the database, with no busy timeout and no retries,
and never reads the process identity; checks running at once do not see each other as holders. The first attempt of
an `acquireProcessLock` running at the same moment still gets a free lock; the later retries of `wait: true` can
find it busy while a check reads it, and get it one backoff later. Without SQLite it reads the lock file and judges
its holder as `acquireProcessLock` does, which reads the process identity, and leaves a dead holder's file for the
next acquisition to reclaim.

1303.content: A held process lock. Releasing it is the caller's job; the lock also ends when the process exits.

1639.content:
An in-memory Platform for tests. Paths are normalized (`//`, `.`, `..` and a trailing `/`); there are no special

that point on the event's lane. A later snapshot on the same lane replaces an earlier one; a field left out was

The payload type of each event kind. Code generic over the kind, such as a function that builds a
`TranscriptEventOf<K>`, types its payload as `TranscriptEventPayloads[K]`: while `K` is a type parameter, TypeScript
does not resolve `TranscriptEventOf<K>['payload']`, so an event built from such a payload does not check as a

One event of a Transcript. Events form a flat list and reference each other by id: `agentId` names a lane in

2014.content: How a model finds its price

2018.content: `/cost` prices usage records with a table you pass in, in USD per million tokens: your own, or the LiteLLM snapshot from `/cost/prices`. It is pure computation and imports nothing. It runs anywhere.

2020.content: `summarize` prices each record using the amount the Agent logged when there is one (Pi, opencode, Grok). Otherwise it prices each count at the model's price (input without cache, cache reads, 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes, output) times the record's `pricingMultiplier` (2 for Codex's priority tier).

2022.content: **Table keys** name one model each. A key prices that id, the id followed by a date (`-20250929`, `-2025-08-07` or Vertex AI's `@20250929`), and either after one `<provider>/` prefix. So `claude-sonnet-4-5` prices `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` and `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5`. Any other ending names another model, so `gpt-5` prices neither `gpt-5.7` nor `gpt-5-codex`.

2023.content: **`fallback`** holds family aliases such as `opus`: an id that no table key matches takes the longest alias its id contains.

2024.content: **`overrides`** are your own rules and, unlike table keys, match by substring: an id takes the longest override key it contains, and that override replaces its prices, also in part, over the table and the fallback. So `{ opus: … }` reprices both `claude-opus-4-8` and `claude-3-opus`, and `{ "gpt-4o": … }` also reaches `gpt-4o-mini`.

2025.content: A partial override takes the prices it lacks from the id's price without overrides: over the snapshot, `{ "gpt-4o": { input: 1 } }` prices `gpt-4o-2024-05-13` at its own output price ($15), not `gpt-4o`'s ($10), and an id without a price of its own stays unpriced.

2026.content: A model without a price has no cost (`undefined`, not 0), and a summary's `costUsd` is absent when nothing in it was priced. A Grok turn split by model is priced and grouped per model.

2027.content: The records come from Token usage. A record carries `costUsd` and `costSource: "agent"` when the log has the Agent's own cost, and `pricingMultiplier` for Codex's priority tier.

2028.content: `priceRecord(record, pricing): PricedRecord` prices one record by the same rules, for a host that adds records to buckets of its own, such as hours.

2029.content: It returns `{ parts }`: one part per model when the record is split by model (`usageByModel`), else one part for the whole record.

2030.content: A part has the `model` (absent when the record names none), its `usage`, its `modelCalls` when it counts them, and its `cost`: `{ costUsd, costSource }`, where `costSource` is `"agent"` for an amount the Agent logged and `"pricing-table"` for one computed from the table.

2031.content: A part that nothing prices has no `cost`, which is not a cost of 0. The parts' costs, added up per Agent and model, are `summarize`'s groups.

2032.content: A part of a split has only the `modelCalls` of its model's share, never the record's: a share that counts none gives a part without `modelCalls`, so the parts can add up to fewer calls than `record.modelCalls`. A host that counts calls per record reads `record.modelCalls` and decides how to divide them among the models.

2033.content: `/cost/prices` is the kit's snapshot of LiteLLM's model price list for the models the supported Agents record. `litellmPrices` is a table for `createPricing`. `litellmPricesVersion` is `<date>+<commit>`: the date (UTC) and commit of LiteLLM's file the snapshot was generated from. Store it with the costs you compute to know which table priced them. The entry imports nothing and is kept apart from `/cost`, so a host that brings its own table does not load this one.

2034.content: The snapshot keeps the chat models of the providers whose own APIs the Agents call: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, xAI, DeepSeek, Z.ai, Moonshot and MiniMax. Its keys are LiteLLM's model names without the provider's own prefix (`grok-4.20`, not `xai/grok-4.20`), because Agents record the bare name; the same models routed through clouds and gateways (`bedrock/…`, `vertex_ai/…`, `openrouter/…`) are left out. Each entry has the input, output, cache write, one-hour cache write and cache read prices that LiteLLM lists. Every Monday a workflow opens a pull request when a price the snapshot keeps has changed, and the next release ships it.

2035.content: Each key names one model, so an id the snapshot has no key for has no price rather than another model's: until the snapshot has `gpt-5.7`, it is unpriced, not priced as `gpt-5`. A host that wants an estimate for such ids passes family aliases in `fallback`, at prices it chooses, or prices the ids with `overrides`. Overrides still match by substring, because the host writes them: a full override keyed `gpt-5` prices `gpt-5.7` and reprices every model the snapshot names whose id contains `gpt-5`; a partial one reprices those models but leaves `gpt-5.7`, which has no price of its own to fill it, unpriced.

2182.content: `@rivus/agent-kit-collab/lanes` exports `createLanes`. It is an Effect entry and is process-local. It needs `effect` at the peer version from Installation. It does not take a platform.

2183.content: Lanes run work per key, one activation at a time, under a global concurrency cap and a bounded queue. The package knows no particular Agent.

2184.content: A lane runs at most one activation at a time. Every wake that arrives before an activation starts is served by it. Waking a running lane any number of times leaves one activation to follow the running one, and waking a queued lane changes nothing.

2185.content: An idle lane starts while a slot is free and nobody waits. Otherwise it waits at the end of the queue, and when `maxQueued` lanes already wait, `wake` fails with `LaneQueueFull`. A freed slot goes to the lane that has waited longest, so a lane woken again while it ran waits behind the lanes queued meanwhile. Without `maxQueued`, the queue holds at most one entry per key.

2186.content: `cancel(key)` drops the wakes the key owes and interrupts its running activation, and returns once the activation has ended (its finalizers and `onExit` included). `close` refuses later wakes with `LanesClosed`, drops the queue, interrupts every running activation and waits for them. Closing the Scope that created the lanes runs it.

2187.content: An activation runs with the context `createLanes` ran in. Its Scope closes when it ends, and the lane moves on only after that. An interrupted activation's finalizers have run before the next activation of any key takes its slot.

2188.content: `onExit` hears how each activation ended. One that succeeded or failed by itself is reported so even when a cancel, close or timeout arrives while its Scope closes. `ActivationInterrupted` means the lanes cut it short, or stopped it before it started, in which case `activate` was never called. `onExit` runs uninterruptibly, so `cancel` and `close` wait for it. It must not wait for them in turn, and a defect it raises is logged as a warning.

2189.content: Nothing is persisted. Lanes live in one process.

2190.content: Expected failures are typed values with a `_tag`: `LaneQueueFull`, `LanesClosed` and `LanesConfigInvalid`.

2191.content: `wake` returns `"started"`, `"queued"` or `"coalesced"` and never waits for the activation. `onExit` reports `ActivationSucceeded`, `ActivationFailed` or `ActivationInterrupted`.

2193.content: One owner per task, with a fencing token that never goes backwards.

2197.content: `@rivus/agent-kit-collab/lease` exports `createLeaseManager`, `LeaseRepository`, `sqliteLeaseRepository`, `fileLeaseRepository` and `memoryLeaseRepository`. It is an Effect entry and needs a platform. It needs `effect` at the peer version from Installation.

2198.content: A lease lets one process at a time own a task, and refuses a stale owner's writes. The package knows no particular Agent.

2199.content: A lease has one holder. Its generation, the fencing token, grows on every acquisition and never goes back. A release keeps the record as a tombstone. Losing the lease and getting it again gives a new generation, so the old handle's token is refused.

2200.content: The holder renews every `heartbeatMs` in the Scope that acquired it. `heartbeatMs × 2` must not exceed `ttlMs`. Closing the Scope stops the heartbeat and releases the lease.

2201.content: A holder on the same host whose process is gone (or whose pid now belongs to another process) is taken over at once. A holder that is alive but stopped renewing is taken over after the TTL, measured by the observer's own monotonic clock from the moment it first saw the current record.

2202.content: `runFenced` holds the repository's per-key fence and re-reads the record before the work starts. Waiting for the fence stops when the lease is lost. The fence is released when the work's fiber ends, so a successor's fenced work starts after that. An interrupted fiber ends at once, but a Promise it started keeps running. Put a write that cannot be cancelled in `Effect.uninterruptible` (the fence then waits for it to settle), or pass it the AbortSignal that `Effect.tryPromise` provides and let it settle only once the write has stopped.

2203.content: Guard plus re-read is as strong as a check by the protected resource itself only when every writer goes through the same repository on the same machine. A resource that can compare atomically should keep the highest token it has seen and reject a smaller generation.

2204.content: `sqliteLeaseRepository` compares revisions inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transactions. `fileLeaseRepository` is the fallback without SQLite: one JSON file per key, written under a per-key lock file. `memoryLeaseRepository` serves one process.

2205.content: The repository port follows the kit's repository shape. `load(key)` is the stored `LeaseSnapshot` or `undefined`, and `save(key, snapshot, expectedRevision)` writes only over that revision and fails with a `RevisionConflict` when another writer moved the record first.

2206.content: Expected failures are typed values with a `_tag`: `LeaseHeld`, `LeaseLost`, `LeaseConfigInvalid`, `LeaseRepositoryFailure` and the repository's `RevisionConflict`. The kit runs no Effect itself. Run the program at your application's assembly root.

2207.content: Holders are judged by host name, boot id, pid and start time. See Installation for win32, NFS, containers and a renamed host.

2209.content: One running instance per machine, with acquireProcessLock.

2213.content: `@rivus/agent-kit-collab/process-lock` exports `acquireProcessLock`, `isProcessLockHeld`, `ProcessLock` and `ProcessLockPlatform`. It is plain TypeScript and takes a platform.

2214.content: A process lock is a single-instance lock for processes that run coding Agents side by side. The package knows no particular Agent.

2215.content: With `platform.sqlite` the lock is a SQLite database held with `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`. The kernel drops it the moment the holder exits or crashes, and nothing is reclaimed. The holder's identity goes into `<path>.holder` for diagnostics only, so a process that cannot read its own identity (`platform.process.self` throws, as on macOS in a sandbox that denies running `ps` or `sysctl`) still takes the lock: `lock.value.holder` is then `undefined`, no `<path>.holder` is written, and one left by a holder that died is removed.

2216.content: Without SQLite the lock is a file that holds the identity. A lock file whose holder died on this host is reclaimed on the next attempt, one reclaimer at a time. The lock file needs the identity to judge its holder, so there `acquireProcessLock` rejects with the error reading it and creates nothing.

2218.content: A crash between creating the lock file and writing the stamp leaves an empty file that counts as held for 30 s.

2219.content: A holder stalled longer than that between the two steps can end up holding the lock together with its reclaimer.

2220.content: Pass `{ wait: true, signal }` to wait for the holder instead of getting `ProcessLockHeld` at once.

2221.content: On win32 the platform cannot identify processes (boot id, pid and start time). A SQLite process lock is still taken, with `holder` undefined. See Installation for NFS, containers and a renamed host.

2222.content: Acquisitions of one lock inside a process take turns in memory, so a lock can be taken from many concurrent tasks without a queue of your own. While one task holds the lock or is attempting it, the next waits for it to release the lock or give up, and only then makes its own attempt. It never opens SQLite against a holder in its own process, whose busy wait would block the thread the holder needs to finish and release.

2223.content: Without `wait` such a call gets `ProcessLockHeld` at once. Aborting `signal` takes a task out of the queue and leaves the others' turns as they were.

2224.content: Tasks share the turns when they name the same file (its directory resolved through symlinks) through platforms with the same `sqlite` object (without SQLite, the same `fs`), as every platform from `createNodePlatform` has. Other processes are still kept out by SQLite or the lock file.

2225.content: The turns live in this package's module state, so a second copy of it in the process (another version, or one bundled into a dependency) does not share them and meets the first in SQLite, as another process does.

2226.content: `isProcessLockHeld` tells whether another process, or an acquisition in this one, holds the lock, without taking it. A short-lived process can use it to hand work to a running holder and start one only when there is none.

2227.content: The check writes nothing: no `<path>.holder`, and a missing lock file reads as free and stays missing.

2228.content: With SQLite it makes one attempt at a shared lock, with no busy timeout and no retries, reads no process identity, and answers in well under a millisecond. Checks that run at once all see a free lock as free. The first attempt of an `acquireProcessLock` running at the same moment waits out a check (a 10 ms busy timeout, then a few short retries) and still gets a free lock. The later retries of `wait: true` have no busy timeout, so one that meets a check can find the free lock busy. The call then gets it after another backoff.

2229.content: Without SQLite it judges the lock file's holder as an acquisition does and leaves a dead holder's file for the next acquisition to reclaim.

2230.content: The answer can be stale by the time it arrives, so only `acquireProcessLock` decides who holds the lock. It takes `{ signal }`. Since the check never waits, it looks at the signal once, before it starts, and rejects with `signal.reason` if it is aborted.

orderedDocs: **`fallback`** holds family aliases such as `opus`: an id that no table key matches takes the longest alias its id contains.

**`overrides`** are your own rules and, unlike table keys, match by substring: an id takes the longest override key it contains, and that override replaces its prices, also in part, over the table and the fallback. So `{ opus: … }` reprices both `claude-opus-4-8` and `claude-3-opus`, and `{ "gpt-4o": … }` also reaches `gpt-4o-mini`.

**Table keys** name one model each. A key prices that id, the id followed by a date (`-20250929`, `-2025-08-07` or Vertex AI's `@20250929`), and either after one `<provider>/` prefix. `@rivus/agent-kit` connects to one Agent at a time. It is a universal Agent toolkit: it knows each Agent's id and home directory, lists its sessions, and reads their logs into one transcript model with one usage convention. Claude Code, Codex and Grok are today's built-in Agents, along with the others on Supported Agents.

`@rivus/agent-kit` is a peer dependency, so the process holds one copy of the platform types. The Effect entries `/lease` and `/lanes` need the host to install `effect` at exactly the version in `peerDependencies.effect`, as reported by the command above. Plain entries do not need this optional peer.

`/cost` prices usage records with a table you pass in, in USD per million tokens: your own, or the LiteLLM snapshot from `/cost/prices`. It is pure computation and imports nothing. It runs anywhere.

`cancel(key)` drops the wakes the key owes and interrupts its running activation, and returns once the activation has ended (its finalizers and `onExit` included). `close` refuses later wakes with `LanesClosed`, drops the queue, interrupts every running activation and waits for them. Closing the Scope that created the lanes runs it.

`command`: the agent runs a command with the payload as JSON on stdin and reads its exit code and stdout.
`plugin`: the agent calls an in-process plugin, which forwards each event's object as the payload.

`connectAgent` starts an Agent's ACP program with exactly the environment you pass, completes the handshake and returns a connection that belongs to your Scope. Closing the Scope closes its sessions and stops the process.

`content-hash`: each new or changed hook definition waits for the user's review, so a command that embeds a
version asks again after every upgrade. `workspace`: hooks run once their folder is trusted, with no per-hook
review.

`detectAgents(platform)` reports, for each built-in Agent in the Agents table, whether it is `runnable`, `found`, `missing` or `unknown`, with the evidence, the version its command printed and the login state.
`detectAgents` reports `found` from a command on PATH, an application path, or an Agent-owned state path.
`detectAgents` resolves to `Installation[]`. A failed probe is recorded in that Agent's `problems`.

`fallback` keys are family aliases, used only when no table key matches: a model takes the longest fallback key its
id contains, the first given among equally long keys, so `opus` prices `claude-opus-4-9` and `gpt-5` prices
`gpt-5.7`.
`hookDialectConformance` checks a hook dialect. `probeRecipeConformance` checks a discovery recipe. How descriptors merge is on Providers.

`isProcessLockHeld` tells whether another process, or an acquisition in this one, holds the lock, without taking it. A short-lived process can use it to hand work to a running holder and start one only when there is none.

`listSessions` reads only the head and tail of each file. It yields `{ ref, error }` for a missing root (`RootMissing`) or an unreadable file (`ReadFailed`) and goes on with the next one. Naming an Agent without a session adapter in `listSessions({ agents })` throws an `AgentKitError` with `code: "capability-unsupported"`.

`listSessions` yields `{ ref, error }` for a missing root (`RootMissing`) or an unreadable file (`ReadFailed`) and goes on with the next one. `scanUsage` yields `{ agent, path, error }` items the same way.

`loadTranscript` and `summarizeSession` resolve to a `Result`: `{ ok: true, value }` or `{ ok: false, error }`, where `error._tag` names the failure. `loadTranscript` and `summarizeSession` fail with `SessionNotFound`, `ReadFailed`, `UnknownFormatGeneration`, `NoAdapterAccepted` or `CapabilityUnsupported`.

`loadTranscript` and `summarizeSession` resolve to a `Result`: `{ ok: true, value }` or `{ ok: false, error }`, where `error._tag` names the failure. They fail with `SessionNotFound`, `ReadFailed`, `UnknownFormatGeneration`, `NoAdapterAccepted` or `CapabilityUnsupported`.

`loadTranscript` reads every file of one session and returns its ordered `events`, its subagent lanes (`agents`) and the records it skipped. It returns the complete session. There is no live file-following API, and a compaction marks the events it replaced with `shadowedBy` only after the whole session is read.

`onExit` hears how each activation ended. One that succeeded or failed by itself is reported so even when a cancel, close or timeout arrives while its Scope closes. `ActivationInterrupted` means the lanes cut it short, or stopped it before it started, in which case `activate` was never called. `onExit` runs uninterruptibly, so `cancel` and `close` wait for it. It must not wait for them in turn, and a defect it raises is logged as a warning.

`overrides` are the caller's own rules and, unlike table keys, match by substring: a model takes the longest
override key its id contains, the first given among equally long keys, and that override wins over the table and
the fallback, so `{ opus: … }` reprices both `claude-opus-4-8` and `claude-3-opus`. A partial override takes the
prices it lacks from the price the id has without overrides: over a table with `gpt-4o` and `gpt-4o-2024-05-13`,
`{ "gpt-4o": { input: 1 } }` keeps the dated model's own output price. A partial override of an id without a price
of its own gives no price. An override entry that says nothing about `longContext` keeps the model's own tier, and
one with a `longContext` replaces it. A model that nothing prices has no price. Lookups are cached by model id.

`phase` is `start`, `activity`, `blocked`, `finish` or `unknown`, with `scope`, `outcome` and `blocker` where the Agent says more. A payload or event the dialect does not know reads as `unknown` instead of throwing. `readHookEvent` never throws because of a payload.
`priceRecord(record, pricing): PricedRecord` prices one record by the same rules, for a host that adds records to buckets of its own, such as hours.
`probeAgent` opens one trial session and reports `ready`, `needs-login` or `unavailable`.
`ready` until it is applied or discarded.

`runFenced` holds the repository's per-key fence and re-reads the record before the work starts. Waiting for the fence stops when the lease is lost. The fence is released when the work's fiber ends, so a successor's fenced work starts after that. An interrupted fiber ends at once, but a Promise it started keeps running. Put a write that cannot be cancelled in `Effect.uninterruptible` (the fence then waits for it to settle), or pass it the AbortSignal that `Effect.tryPromise` provides and let it settle only once the write has stopped.
`scanUsage` reads every Agent's usage under its home and returns a state to pass to the next scan, which then reads only what was written since.

`scanUsage` with a kept state yields only what was written since. A caller that keeps a state also keeps its own totals beside it, uses one state per window with the same `since`, and runs its scans one at a time: two concurrent scans from one state both yield the new records. The scan itself is on Token usage.
`scanUsage` yields `{ agent, path, error }` items for a failed read and goes on. OpenCode's SQLite store needs `platform.sqlite`. Without it a scan yields `SqliteUnavailable`.
`session/new`; fails with `AuthRequired` when the agent needs a login first.
`sessionAdapterHome` resolves a session or usage service's home. Direct usage decoding calls it as `sessionAdapterHome(usage, { home, env })`. See Token usage.
`sessionKey` binds a key to the session in the `SessionBindingStore` (`MemorySessionBindingStoreLive` or `FileSessionBindingStoreLive(path)`), so a later connection can `loadSession({ sessionKey })`.
`sqlite` when the platform has SQLite; `file` is the weaker fallback (see `acquireProcessLock`).

`sqliteLeaseRepository` compares revisions inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transactions. `fileLeaseRepository` is the fallback without SQLite: one JSON file per key, written under a per-key lock file. `memoryLeaseRepository` serves one process.

`summarize` prices each record using the amount the Agent logged when there is one (Pi, opencode, Grok). Otherwise it prices each count at the model's price (input without cache, cache reads, 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes, output) times the record's `pricingMultiplier` (2 for Codex's priority tier).

`summarizeSession` reads the Agent's bounded summarize pass where it has one and folds the loaded transcript otherwise, with the same numbers either way. The pass's memory grows with the session's requests, lanes and tool calls, not with the file's bytes.
`terminal` names the herdr, cmux, Superset or tmux pane the hook ran in.
`uninstall("my-app")` removes only what the ledger records and keeps files the user changed.
`wake` returns `"started"`, `"queued"` or `"coalesced"` and never waits for the activation. `onExit` reports `ActivationSucceeded`, `ActivationFailed` or `ActivationInterrupted`.
+1 on every write; stores compare it to write only over the record a caller read.

A `system` event with `type: 'prompt_snapshot'`: the system prompt and tool definitions the agent recorded at
that point on the event's lane. A later snapshot on the same lane replaces an earlier one; a field left out was
not recorded by that snapshot. `promptSnapshot` returns it for such an event.
A `UsageRecord` is one model request (`granularity: "request"`), or a turn when the Agent logs only turn totals (Grok, with `modelCalls` and `usageByModel`).

A caller that keeps a state also keeps its own totals beside it, uses one state per window with the same `since`, and runs its scans one at a time: two concurrent scans from one state both yield the new records. Counts follow the usage convention.
A check that could not complete. Detection goes on; the problem is reported with the installation.
A confirmation the agent will ask the user for after installation. A plan announces it and never approves it.
A count the log does not record is absent, not 0.
A crash between creating the lock file and writing the stamp leaves an empty file that counts as held for 30 s.
A custom `identity` supplies aliases and a fallback home rule. Conflicting aliases, or an identity whose id differs from its descriptor, are rejected.

A faster pass than folding the loaded transcript, with the same result: no transcript or event payload is kept,
and the state it holds grows with the session's requests, lanes and tool calls, never with its bytes. With
`prompts`, the summary also carries the main lane's user prompts under the given caps, by the same rule
`sessionPrompts` applies to the loaded transcript — an implementation that leaves them out fails the conformance
suite. The equality covers the summary's numbers and prompts, not the failure modes: the pass may read fewer
files than `load` (side files the summary's numbers never read) and in its own order, so an IO error on one of
those can fail `load` while `summarize` succeeds, or the reverse.

A file in which the agent keeps its own copy of what it registered, such as a plugin's hooks in Codex's plugin
cache. When set, an active registration's content is that file's text: a registration whose copy is outdated is
unregistered and registered again, and verify compares the copy the agent runs. A disabled registration stays

or crashes, so the next process takes it at once and probes the pending operations. The holder writes its identity

win32 is not supported: the platform cannot identify processes there (boot id, pid and start time), which leases and lock files need. A SQLite process lock is still taken, with `holder` undefined, as described in Process locks.

With `platform.sqlite` it makes one attempt at a shared lock on the database, with no busy timeout and no retries,
and never reads the process identity; checks running at once do not see each other as holders. The first attempt of
an `acquireProcessLock` running at the same moment still gets a free lock; the later retries of `wait: true` can
find it busy while a check reads it, and get it one backoff later. Without SQLite it reads the lock file and judges
its holder as `acquireProcessLock` does, which reads the process identity, and leaves a dead holder's file for the
next acquisition to reclaim.

With `platform.sqlite` the lock is a SQLite database held with `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`. The kernel drops it the moment the holder exits or crashes, and nothing is reclaimed. The holder's identity goes into `<path>.holder` for diagnostics only, so a process that cannot read its own identity (`platform.process.self` throws, as on macOS in a sandbox that denies running `ps` or `sysctl`) still takes the lock: `lock.value.holder` is then `undefined`, no `<path>.holder` is written, and one left by a holder that died is removed.

With SQLite it makes one attempt at a shared lock, with no busy timeout and no retries, reads no process identity, and answers in well under a millisecond. Checks that run at once all see a free lock as free. The first attempt of an `acquireProcessLock` running at the same moment waits out a check (a 10 ms busy timeout, then a few short retries) and still gets a free lock. The later retries of `wait: true` have no busy timeout, so one that meets a check can find the free lock busy. The call then gets it after another backoff.
Without `wait` such a call gets `ProcessLockHeld` at once. Aborting `signal` takes a task out of the queue and leaves the others' turns as they were.
Without a version probe, the agent is at most `found`.
Without SQLite it judges the lock file's holder as an acquisition does and leaves a dead holder's file for the next acquisition to reclaim.

Without SQLite the lock is a file that holds the identity. A lock file whose holder died on this host is reclaimed on the next attempt, one reclaimer at a time. The lock file needs the identity to judge its holder, so there `acquireProcessLock` rejects with the error reading it and creates nothing.

Writes into files that agents and other tools share are not compare-and-swap: a writer that does not take the
LedgerLock can still change a file between the re-check and the write, and that change is lost without a trace.
